name: Castor oil lashes

lead: Castor oil is brushed along the lash line by people hoping for longer, fuller lashes. It is cheap, easy to find, and widely shown in social media beauty content.

Users credit its moisture and conditioning for the result, and the coating makes lashes look glossier and darker right away. No clinical trial has shown it increases lash growth, and the only product approved for lash growth in the sources is bimatoprost.

paras: People apply a thin layer with a clean spoolie or applicator along the lash line, usually at night, and repeat it over weeks as part of a routine. Many keep using it for the conditioned look.

Topical castor oil is generally low-risk, with rare contact dermatitis reported. Summaries note that non-sterile oil in the eye can cause irritation, infection or corneal damage, so it needs to stay out of the eye.

angle.text: Users brush castor oil along the lash line to make lashes look longer, thicker and darker. The oil coats the hairs for an immediate glossy look, and proponents credit its moisture for fuller lashes over time. No trial has shown it grows lashes.

lead: Castor oil on eyelashes is a folk practice in which castor oil, pressed from Ricinus communis seeds, is brushed along the lash line in the belief that it lengthens or thickens lashes. It is common in social media beauty content and in looksmaxxing discussion of lashes and brows.[1][2]

A general reference work on castor oil states that no high-quality clinical trials show it stimulates eyelash growth, and that thickening claims rest on user reports.[2] The only prescription product approved for eyelash growth named in the sources is bimatoprost (Latisse).[2][3]

paras: Castor oil is about 90 percent ricinoleic acid and has been used medicinally since antiquity and as an emollient in cosmetics.[1] Eyelash length is largely genetic, with upper lashes typically 7 to 8 mm, and the number of follicles is fixed before birth.[4]

Proponents describe castor oil as improving the moisture, circulation or strength of lashes and brows.[2] A reference summary reports that reviews find at most weak or indirect evidence for improved hair luster through coating of the strands, which could make lashes look glossier without changing growth, and that ricinoleic acid's effect on prostaglandin D2 has been studied for scalp hair loss but not demonstrated for eyelashes.[2]

Topical castor oil is generally considered low-risk and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review has deemed it safe in leave-on products, though rare contact dermatitis has been reported, particularly with undiluted use.[2] The same summary advises that non-sterile castor oil should not be put in the eyes because of risks of irritation, infection and corneal damage.[2]
No studies found. A 2021 randomized trial of castor oil applied to the eyelids tested it for blepharitis, not lash growth, and reported improved eyelid signs without adverse events.[2]
